entries.subject: biology
entries.statement: Osmosis is when water moves to where there is more water.
entries.correct: Water moves across a selectively permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration (down the water potential gradient) - i.e. toward more solute, not more water.
entries.source: Odom, A.L. & Barrow, L.H. (1995), 'Development and application of a two-tier diagnostic test measuring college biology students' understanding of diffusion and osmosis', Journal of Research in Science Teaching 32(1).

source_check.by: assistant, 2026-10-27, web search of bibliographic records and papers that cite it; the papers were not read in full; not reviewed by a person
source_check.note: Odom and Barrow created the Diffusion and Osmosis Diagnostic Test in 1995, per later papers that cite it. The journal record itself (volume, pages) was not found in this check.

entries.subject: chemistry
entries.statement: Ionic and covalent bonds are basically the same kind of sharing.
entries.correct: Ionic bonding is electron TRANSFER between a metal and non-metal (forming ions held by electrostatic attraction); covalent bonding is electron SHARING between non-metals. The electronegativity difference decides which occurs.
entries.source: Taber, K.S. (1998), 'An alternative conceptual framework from chemistry education', International Journal of Science Education 20(5); and Taber & Coll (2002) on chemical bonding alternative conceptions.

source_check.by: assistant, 2026-10-27, web search of bibliographic records and papers that cite it; the papers were not read in full; not reviewed by a person
source_check.note: The 1998 paper exists (IJSE 20(5), 597-608, doi 10.1080/0950069980200507). Secondary sources say it describes ionic bonding as electron transfer within the octet framework.

entries.subject: physics
entries.statement: A moving object needs a continuous force to keep moving.
entries.correct: An object in motion stays in motion at constant velocity unless acted on by a net external force (Newton's first law). What stops everyday objects is friction, not the absence of a driving force.
entries.source: Clement, J. (1982), 'Students' preconceptions in introductory mechanics', American Journal of Physics 50(1); and Halloun & Hestenes (1985), 'Common sense concepts about motion', American Journal of Physics 53(11).

source_check.by: assistant, 2026-10-27, web search of bibliographic records and papers that cite it; the papers were not read in full; not reviewed by a person
source_check.note: Both papers exist: Clement 1982 (AJP 50(1), 66-71, doi 10.1119/1.12989) and Halloun and Hestenes 1985 (AJP 53(11), 1056-1065), the latter a taxonomy of common-sense beliefs about motion. Clement's text was not read.

entries.subject: biology
entries.statement: Plants take in their food from the soil through their roots.
entries.correct: Plants make their own food (glucose) by photosynthesis in the leaves, using carbon dioxide, water and light energy. The soil supplies water and mineral ions, not food.
entries.source: Driver, R. et al. (1994), 'Making Sense of Secondary Science: Research into Children's Ideas', Routledge.

source_check.by: assistant, 2026-10-27, web search of bibliographic records and papers that cite it; the papers were not read in full; not reviewed by a person
source_check.note: The book exists (Driver, Squires, Rushworth, Wood-Robinson; Routledge; 1993 or 1994 by listing). Its passage on plants taking food from soil was not found in this check.

entries.subject: physics
entries.statement: Current is used up as it goes around a circuit, so less comes back to the cell.
entries.correct: Charge is conserved: the current is the same at every point in a simple series circuit. What is transferred to the components is energy, not current.
entries.source: Shipstone, D. (1984), 'A study of children's understanding of electricity in simple DC circuits', European Journal of Science Education 6(2).

source_check.by: assistant, 2026-10-27, web search of bibliographic records and papers that cite it; the papers were not read in full; not reviewed by a person
